item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers dynasty is over, or has at least hit a major bump in the road. Thursday's Game 4 loss to the Milwaukee Brewers completed the four-game sweep and sent the two-time defending World Series champions home for the winter. Los Angeles' season is over, as is its stretch of eight consecutive postseason series wins dating back to 2024.
There is no getting around it: The Dodgers looked old in the NLCS. They are old too. Weighed by playing time, they had baseball's oldest collection of position players this season. Will Smith is 31. Shohei Ohtani is 32. Mookie Betts and Teoscar Hernández are 34. Freddie Freeman is 37. The team's core hitters are getting long in the tooth. It was obvious in the NLCS.
That said, the Dodgers remain extremely talented and have the resources (money and tradeable prospects) to improve their roster in the offseason, and again contend in 2027. As bad as they looked in the NLCS, there is no reason to think the Dodgers won't be among baseball's best teams next year -- and on the short list of legitimate World Series contenders.
Here now are three questions facing the Dodgers following their unceremonious NLCS sweep.
1. What is Shohei Ohtani's future?
The two-way star was hindered by health for a large chunk of 2026
In fact, let's talk about his future both short- and long-term. Ohtani was clearly diminished late in the regular season and into the postseason. He played through knee and biceps injuries and simply did not look like himself at the plate. His swing was all arms and there was little hard contact. Before his second-inning home run in Game 4 on Thursday, Ohtani hadn't gone deep since Aug. 18. His power vanished.
Here is Ohtani's expected slugging percentage, which is based on contact quality (exit velocity, launch angle, etc.), throughout this season. It slipped significantly late in the year:
Ohtani did not pitch after July 3 and had a start-and-stop in late August. He rehabbed his injuries, threw bullpen sessions and live batting practice, then had to shut it down before getting back on a mound in a game. Ohtani was playing like his usual MVP self until his injuries popped up in the second half. Once that happened, his season began to circle the drain.
The Dodgers now face two questions with Ohtani. One, does he need offseason surgery on the knee and/or biceps? And if he does need surgery, will the recovery cut into his 2027? Keep in mind that it is a near certainty there will be a lockout this offseason once the CBA expires on Dec. 1, and teams will be banned from communicating with their players. Ohtani would have to rehab on his own, without the team's input.
"It's hard to tell" if he'll require surgery, Ohtani said through an interpreter after Thursday's loss. He does, however, plan to pitch next season, he said.
Offseason surgery is the short-term question. Long-term, regardless of what he said in the shadow of the NLCS sweep, are Ohtani's days as a pitcher numbered? This has been a question since Day 1 of Ohtani's MLB career. His ability to be and remain a two-way player has long been doubted, but he has kept doing it, even if there have been some speed bumps along the way. Ohtani has made a career of doing what people said he couldn't.
The man is 32 now, though. He'll turn 33 next summer and the physical ailments (the knee, the biceps, two UCL surgeries, etc.) are beginning to add up. At some point, Ohtani won't be able to continue as a two-way player, and with each passing season, that point draws closer. Are we there now? Is this it? Is this the end of Ohtani's time as a pitcher? It could be, sure.
My guess is that Ohtani will continue to pitch next season and the Dodgers will happily let him because there is so much value to be gained even if he throws only 75 innings a year. You can't be as good as Ohtani without being stubborn. He's been stubborn in that he insists on playing both ways, and he has continued to do it well. I don't see him dropping it this winter.
It should surprise no one if Ohtani comes out next year, hits 40 home runs, makes 15 ace-caliber starts and wins his fifth MVP unanimously. Do not forget that he was playing at that level as recently as July. The recovery times for the knee and biceps injuries are an offseason question, for sure, and the bottom line is the "will he continue to pitch?" questions will always exist.
2. Will they move on from some longtime stalwarts?
Could the Dodgers say goodbye to Teoscar Hernández or some other familiar names?
The Dodgers are locked into so much of their core: Betts, Freeman, Ohtani, Smith, Kyle Tucker, etc. They aren't going anywhere. That said, there are a few members of the supporting cast, players who have been around for all three recent World Series wins, who might have to be shown the door this offseason for the sake of diversifying the lineup and getting younger and more athletic.
Finding a taker for the final season of Teoscar Hernández's contract and then plugging the precocious Josue De Paula into left field next season is a worthwhile move. It's difficult because Hernández is popular in the clubhouse, but, on the field, De Paula figures to give the Dodgers a better chance to win ballgames moving forward. (De Paula is a poor defender, but so is Hernández.)
The Enrique Hernández era has run its course. He hasn't been even an average regular-season player since 2022, and, for all his postseason heroics, he's barely scraping a .600 OPS in the last two Octobers. Tommy Edman is a better version of the same player. There's no need to carry both on the roster, plus Edman's injuries suggest a smaller role is needed. Less could be more.
Max Muncy stayed healthy this season, hit 29 homers and posted 4.1 WAR, and is owed an affordable $10 million in 2027. Plus, it's a bad offseason to need an infielder. The free-agent market is very thin and you're not likely to find better than Muncy on the trade market. Still, he is 36. Keeping Muncy is justifiable, but it also makes sense to explore alternatives. It never hurts to look.
Blake Treinen has not been healthy and effective at the same time in two years. Alex Vesia's fastball sat 91-92 mph over these last few weeks. Both are free agents and the Dodgers have so many young hard-throwers in Triple-A that I think it's worth turning the page and injecting some younger arms into the bullpen. Evan Phillips may be in this camp, too.
Then again, who am I to doubt the Dodgers and their process? Disappointing NLCS aside, they have been baseball's most successful team of the 2020s, and if they want to remain in the Hernández and Muncy and Treinen business, I won't say they're wrong. It does appear that things are getting a bit stale, though. Incorporating youth would be sensible, and it isn't difficult to find ways to do it.
3. Will they retain Tarik Skubal?
It will cost a lot to keep the trade deadline addition atop the rotation
There's no sense in asking if the Dodgers can retain Tarik Skubal. Of course they can. They are baseball's biggest spenders and he is a Scott Boras client. Typically, all you need to do to get a Boras client is make the biggest offer, which the Dodgers can do. Maybe there's a salary cap that changes the equation. Based on what we know right now, yes, the Dodgers can, of course, re-sign Skubal.
Will they is a different matter. Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will return next season. Ohtani could be back on the mound as well, as he indicated is the plan. Emmet Sheehan and Justin Wrobleski both pitched well for long stretches this year and are among the very best No. 5 starter options in the game. Gavin Stone, the team's 2024 innings leader, should return from shoulder surgery as well.
There is never a bad time to sign a pitcher like Skubal, and the Dodgers, with their World Series window still open, are well-positioned to bring him back. They have the money, they can easily clear rotation space, and all indications are that Skubal enjoyed his time with the team after coming over the trade deadline. This feels like a match made in free-agent heaven.
Now it's just a matter of whether the Dodgers can get it done. Perhaps a salary cap or increased competitive balance tax penalties limit their spending; maybe they opt to spread their money around to multiple players; maybe another team just won't be denied. The Dodgers don't absolutely need Skubal. Re-signing him would up their odds of returning to the World Series, though, and help ensure their dynasty didn't end on Thursday night.
For his part, Skubal declined to comment on his impending decision after Game 4.
"I'm not going to comment on my future really at all," Skubal said, via MLB.com. "Today sucks, you know, and that's kind of where my head's at."

LOS ANGELES — In the end, it was all too much – coming back from a 3-0 deficit, winning a third consecutive World Series championship.
Shohei Ohtani came back to life after two months of ugly at-bats, unfamiliar criticism and questions about whether he even belonged in the Dodgers’ lineup. His three-run home run in the second inning on Thursday night gave the Dodgers a four-run lead – unheard of in this postseason of run suppression.
That wasn’t enough to keep their season alive against a relentless Milwaukee Brewers team that just kept coming, taking a 6-4 win in Game 4 on Thursday to complete a four-game sweep of the two-time defending champions and advance from the National League Championship Series to their first World Series in 44 years.
After falling behind on Garrett Mitchell’s home run off Tanner Scott in the sixth inning, the Dodgers put the tying run on third base with one out in the sixth, seventh and eighth innings but couldn’t move him another 90 feet. Their dreams of a three-peat were buried under another collection of failed at-bats with a runner in scoring position. They went 2 for 11 in those situations in Game 4 and 5 for 43 in the postseason.
“As a manager and anyone participating in the game, you always wonder … could we have done something different that could have changed the game?” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “I think at the end of the day, we got beat. We got outplayed in all facets. Those guys played flawless defensively. They pitched better than we did. They hit better than we did. They slugged more than we did. You’ve got to sometimes just tip your cap.
“I personally told our guys that there’s no apologies, there’s no ‘Sorry’s. We gave it everything we had, and it wasn’t good enough. That’s part of life.”
The New York Yankees of 1998-2000 are still the most recent team to ‘three-peat’ as World Series champions. A National League franchise still hasn’t done it.
“It’s hard to win one. We won two,” Freddie Freeman said. “We went for three and we came up short on a third. Special stuff the past two years. We just came up short this year.”
After losing Game 3 on Wednesday night to become the 42nd team in MLB history to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven series, the Dodgers said all the right things about becoming just the second to climb out of that hole and win the series.
“Four one-game winning streaks,” Dodgers utility player Kiké Hernandez said.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year, ten times, I think,” Manager Dave Roberts said.
Ohtani gave them reason to believe.
With the Brewers rolling out a ‘bullpen game’ in Game 4, opener Shane Drohan was gone after a leadoff single by Kyle Tucker in the second inning. Former Dodger Dustin May replaced him and gave up another single to Teoscar Hernandez, struck out Max Muncy then gave up an RBI single to Andy Pages – the only Dodger who seemed able to hit with a runner in scoring position this postseason.
Kiké Hernandez flew out, bringing Ohtani to the plate with two outs. He struck out against Drohan in the first inning but had finished Game 3 with a 113.5 mph exit velocity on an eighth-inning single – the kind of hard contact missing from Ohtani since mid-August and one of the signs that convinced Roberts to move him back to the leadoff spot for Game 4.
May threw Ohtani a 1-and-1 cutter in at his knees and Ohtani crushed it. It left his bat at 113.1 mph and traveled 428 feet into the right field pavilion. The emotion that burst out of Ohtani was just as explosive. As the crowd roared, he bounced down the first-base line, screaming and gesturing at his teammates in the dugout.
It looked like things were finally turning the Dodgers’ way in this series.
“It’s hard to not say yeah to that,” Muncy said. “He gets that moment, it’s like that’s the swing we’ve been waiting for. We got a nice lead, we got Glas on the mound, we’re confident behind him and they just kept stringing together one good at-bat after another after another after another. They were just kind of relentless.”
The Dodgers’ first home run in the NLCS ended the longest home-run drought of Ohtani’s career at 25 games and 116 plate appearances.
The only thing that seemed longer was how long the Dodgers were going to have to work to make that four-run second inning stand up.
It began disappearing in the fourth inning.
Starter Tyler Glasnow retired the first 10 Brewers in order and struck out six of the first eight. He didn’t have another strikeout. It was nothing but contact from the Brewers after that.
A walk and back-to-back ground-rule doubles – the second by Jake Bauers – cut the Dodgers’ lead in half. An inning later, Glasnow walked the No. 8 hitter, Sal Frelick, who stole second and scored on a single by the No. 9 hitter David Hamilton.
Glasnow was replaced by Evan Phillips who walked three in a row (one intentionally after Hamilton stole second) to force in the tying run.
The four aces the Dodgers thought would give them the upper hand in this postseason did not. Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Glasnow combined for a 6.50 ERA in the series against the Brewers. Only Skubal allowed fewer than three runs in his start.
Tanner Scott came on for the sixth inning. He didn’t give up a home run to a left-handed batter all season. The Brewers’ first batter in the sixth, left-handed Garrett Mitchell, has just two home runs off left-handed pitchers in his 286 career regular-season games.
Scott left a full-count fastball over the heart of the plate and Mitchell, a former UCLA and Orange Lutheran standout, sent it over the center field wall for his second home run off a left-handed pitcher in three at-bats (Blake Snell in Game 3).
The Brewers’ bullpen took over from there. The Dodgers got Kyle Tucker to third base after his one-out double in the sixth, Pages to third after his leadoff double in the seventh and Will Smith to third when Brewers right fielder Frelick fumbled his double in the right field corner.
The six at-bats with a chance to push across the tying run ended in three strikeouts, two ground outs and a shallow pop up to center field.
Hamilton made it a two-run lead with a solo home run in the top of the ninth. It was just the fifth hit of the game for the Brewers.
More to come on this story.

When it comes to lineup decisions, Max Muncy figures to regain a starting role at third base, and you have to wonder if Will Smith remains in the seventh spot—the Dodger catcher was responsible for the only big hit the home team had in a Game 3 loss. Speaking of hitters who moved down in the order, although it amounted to very little, Shohei Ohtani reached safely in three of his four plate appearances in a 6-2 defeat.

The Milwaukee Brewers set the series tone on Sunday night with a narrow victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 1 of the NLCS. Powered by excellent infield defense, which produced three ground-ball double plays, an incredible swing from Brice Turang that led to a game-tying home run off Tarik Skubal, and another dominant performance from their bullpen, Pat Murphy's squad built a key 1-0 series lead in their quest to knock off the reigning back-to-back World Series champs.
After Turang's game-tying solo shot in the fourth, the Brewers took the lead in the bottom of the fifth thanks to an RBI single from rookie right fielder Luis Lara. The Brewers maintained that narrow one-run lead through the final four innings of the series opener, but they certainly had opportunities to add on to their run total.
Milwaukee's best scoring opportunity came in the bottom of the eighth inning. Jackson Chourio led off the inning with a single to right field off right-handed reliever Evan Phillips. After the leadoff hit, Dodgers manager turned to southpaw Tanner Scott to face Brice Turang, who promptly laid down a sacrifice bunt to advance Chourio to second base, setting up an RBI opportunity for William Contreras.
However, with the left-handed Scott on the mound, Roberts elected to intentionally walk Contreras, setting up a tough left-on-left matchup for Jake Bauers. Scott struck out Bauers on six pitches, which brought lefty-crusher Andrew Vaughn to the plate. Once again, Roberts elected to intentionally walk the righty to set up a left-on-left matchup with Garrett Mitchell. In doing so, however, Roberts moved a key insurance run to third base, where a passed ball or wild pitch would have given the Brewers a two-run lead, and a single would have given them a three-run advantage.
It was undoubtedly a risk for Roberts and the Dodgers -- loading the bases for Mitchell -- but one that paid off on Sunday night. However, in doing so, Roberts exposed a strategy he may use throughout the remainder of the series: prioritizing matchups between his left-handed relievers and the Brewers' left-handed hitters. Such a strategy means the Brewers lefties will have to find ways to produce against Los Angeles' tough bullpen southpaws throughout the series.
The pressure is on the Brewers' left-handed hitters to produce against Dodgers' tough lefty relievers
Left-on-left matchups are something the Brewers are bound to see a lot of throughout the NLCS. From starters Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell to a quartet of lefty relievers in Alex Vesia, Tanner Scott, Kris Bubic, and Justin Wrobleski, Milwaukee can expect to see plenty of southpaws throughout their rematch with the Dodgers.
Clearly, based on last night's strategy, Roberts is going to prioritize matching those lefties up with the Brewers' left-handed hitters by any means necessary. That means there will likely be situations, like last night, where Bauers, Mitchell, Brice Turang, and Christian Yelich will be asked to produce against a same-side pitcher. Concerningly for the Brewers, of that group only Bauers (.901 OPS vs. LHP) had an OPS better than .668 against left-handed pitching during the regular season.
Bauers commented on his improved success against left-handed pitching this year during his pre-game press conference on Monday morning, saying, "A lot of it just has to do with getting the opportunity to see them more often, and then I think I've really focused on developing an approach that gives me the best chance."
On the topic of opportunities, Bauers set a new career-high with 160 plate appearances against left-handed pitchers this year, and already that practice against lefties is coming in handy in the NLCS. Bauers acknowledged the difficult southpaws on the Dodgers' NLCS roster, saying, "Some of these guys, obviously it's not easy, whether it be high arm slot coming from behind you or someone throwing from the side," but in four at-bats in Game 1 last night, all of which came against left-handed pitchers, Bauers went 1-for-3 with a walk and a hard-hit single. Pair that with Turang's impressive blast off Skubal, and the Brewers' left-handers are off to a strong start against same-side pitchers in the NLCS.
Assuming Roberts continues to prioritize these matchups, even if it means intentionally putting runners on base, the pressure will be on Bauers, Turang, and the rest of the Brewers' lefties to continue putting together strong at-bats in these situations. If they can find success against southpaws early in the series, it will certainly complicate Roberts' pitching plan going forward.

De cara a su tercera Serie de Campeonato consecutiva en la postemporada de las Grandes Ligas de Béisbol (MLB), los Dodgers tendrían una de las mejores noticias posibles para su relevo con el boricua Edwin Díaz de regreso en su mejor forma, lo que eventualmente le permitirá tomar la mayor cantidad de oportunidades como el cerrador del equipo que busca un tricampeonato en la Serie Mundial.
Sugar endulza el relevo de Dodgers para la SCLN
Díaz, que tuvo una tropezada temporada de debut con los Dodgers por una lesión en el codo y otra más en el cuello, tuvo números atípicos para uno de los mejores cerradores de los últimos años en las Grandes Ligas. De regreso en la Serie de Campeonato, el Sugar completó oportunidades de salvamento consecutivas en el Juego 3 y el Juego 4.
“Las últimas dos noches... esa es la razón por la que adquirimos a alguien como Edwin Díaz”, dijo Roberts después de que los Dodgers ganaran la Serie Divisional. “Es uno de los grandes cerradores del juego. Que esté lanzando a su mejor nivel justo ahora es lo que uno espera, y le doy mucho mérito por ello”.
Si bien Roberts y los Dodgers no ha designado nuevamente a Díaz como su cerrador nuevamente, sí le da una opción más para situaciones de alta exigencia con 8 juegos más por ganar para conquistar el tricampeonato del Clásico de Otoño.
“Creo que eso fue lo más importante para mí: que el equipo confía en mí”, dijo Díaz después del último juego de la SDLN. “Me dan la pelota todos los días... Por eso vine aquí, para ganar partidos y cerrar encuentros como este. Así que estoy muy contento en este momento”.
¿Qué opciones tiene Dodgers en el relevo?
Con Díaz volviendo a su nivel élite, los Dodgers pueden barajear las opciones en juegos de alta exigencia, especialmente con Tanner Scott (25 salvamentos en la temporada regular) y Evan Phillips (un rescate en la campaña).
Scott tiene tiempo para reponerse luego del golpe que puede representar recibir un jonrón de dos carreras en el Juego 1 de la Serie Divisional y después registrar holds –ventajas de 3 o menos carreras sostenidas en relevo intermedio– durante el octavo episodio del Juego 3 y 4. Phillips relevó a Scott para quedarse con el salvamento del Juego 1.
Esas dos opciones sirviendo como preparadores le permiten a los Dodgers jugar a Alex Vesia y Edgardo Henriquez como relevo intermedio; Vesia en duelos de zurdo contra zurdo y el venezolano Henriquez en diestro contra diestro.

LOS ANGELES -- Reliever Evan Phillips was reinstated off the injured list Monday, returning to the Los Angeles Dodgers 13 months after having Tommy John surgery.
The 31-year-old right-hander spent the last month at Triple-A Oklahoma City, where he had a 1.80 ERA with 13 strikeouts and five walks in 10 innings over 12 games for the Comets.
"My primary mix is very sharp and ready to roll," he said before the Dodgers defeated the Colorado Rockies8-7 in 11 innings.
Phillips, who did not appear in Monday's win, had the surgery in May 2025, setting him on course for the first long-term rehab stint of his career.
"Credit to myself to stick with the process, leaning a lot on my family and my teammates here," he said. "I was very appreciative to spend my rehab here last year after the injury. I think that helped my mindset stay focused as well. Just ready for this next step."
Phillips won't be needed again in the closer role. Tanner Scott has been ably filling in for injured Edwin Díaz, who went on the IL in April for loose bodies in his elbow.
Phillips figures to slot into a middle-relief position as he builds up to a potentially bigger role in October, when the NL West-leading Dodgers are expected to seek a third consecutive World Series championship.
During his month in the minors, Phillips spent his first several games focused on the physical side of pitching, including experimenting with grips, location, and working on a changeup. Then he flipped the switch.
"The second half of it I really tried to step up the execution and competition side of things," he said. "That way, hopefully, it's not the first time I'm doing it here."
In a corresponding move, the Dodgers optioned right-hander Paul Gervase to Triple-A a day after he tossed two scoreless innings with two strikeouts against San Diego. Left-hander Jake Eder was released.
In other moves, the team added pitcher Carlos Duran to the 40-man roster and designated catcher Chuckie Robinson for assignment.
Duran, a 24-year-old right-hander, appeared in 30 games for Triple-A Oklahoma City, going 2-2 with a 3.86 ERA this season. He had 50 strikeouts in 35 innings while limiting hitters to a .203 average. He made his major league debut last season with the Athletics.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts ruled pitcher Blake Treinen out for the postseason after the right-hander suffered a shoulder injury warming up for a relief appearance in San Francisco.
Now, it sounds as if Roberts spoke prematurely.
Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said Saturday that Treinen's status for the postseason is "not decided firmly."
"It was clear for this round," Friedman said, "but we'll keep monitoring it as we go."
Friedman described the injury as "soreness" — a vague if much less ominous problem than the one Roberts suggested when Treinen was placed on the injured list after the Dodgers' Sept. 26 game against the Giants.
“I don't know if it was a complete blowout, but really unfortunate,” Roberts said at the time.
In 12 MLB seasons — the last six with the Dodgers — Treinen is 49-42 with a 2.94 ERA and 83 saves. Although he served as the Dodgers' closer only occasionally, he was a reliable source of strikeouts, low ERAs and some big postseason moments as the Dodgers captured three World Series championships this decade.
In 2024, Treinen saved three postseason games in three opportunities, allowing only three runs across nine October appearances. He was the winning pitcher in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series, when he threw 2.1 scoreless relief innings against the New York Yankees.
If the Dodgers need Treinen this month, it won't merely mean that he is healthy. It will mean somebody else — likely a couple somebodies — are not.
The Dodgers have enough quality and capable bullpen arms that they did not roster two pitchers who figured to be October mainstays (left-handers Justin Wrobleski and Jack Dreyer) in the National League Division Series. That decision was made in large part due to the Dodgers' opponent.
For Treinen to appear in a game this month, he'd have to prove more worthy of a roster spot than Tanner Scott, Alex Vesia, Brock Stewart, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Edgardo Henriquez, Edwin Diaz and Kris Bubic — plus Wrobleski and Dreyer.
Right-handers Bobby Miller and Emmet Sheehan have lockers and figure to be ready if called upon, too. Right-hander Will Klein finished the season on the injured list, like Treinen, but his throwing progression has put him in position to rejoin the roster if needed.
Treinen's possible availability is likely a mere footnote to the Dodgers' 2026 postseason run. Considering it sounded impossible a week ago, it's at least worth noting.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are eyeing a historic three-peat, and it's going to take an incredible pitching staff to do so.
This team's offense is what it is, but there are still questions regarding the bullpen, specifically at the end of games.
Manager Dave Roberts recently had a chance to speak with the media, and according to Dodgers Nation, he's confident in four different players to close out games this October.
Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, and Edwin Diaz were all named by one of the best skippers the league has ever seen, but ultimately it will come down to what Roberts is feeling in each given situation, along with how each reliever has performed up to that point.
Dodgers can afford to be flexible
At this point in the year, all bets are off. Starting pitchers come in as relievers, closers are asked to open games, simply put, everything is on the table.
Going into the National League Division Series, Roberts said it's "easy to see" Scott finishing games.
He then added that will vary by game, and if an opportunity presents itself to use Scott in the eighth inning, that's exactly what this team will do.
The Dodgers are the back-to-back World Series Champions for a reason, and it's partly due to the brilliant mind that Roberts has.
He said he feels "very comfortable" with Sasaki, Phillips, and Diaz closing out games.
Diaz's struggles have been well-documented, though injuries may have played a huge part in all of that.
Phillips has just one save this season, but that doesn't mean the 32-year-old isn't built for the bright lights.
Finally, Sasaki will remain a mainstay of this team's bullpen in a similar role to what he did a year ago with his three postseason saves and two holds in nine appearances.
Is Scott the obvious choice?
On paper, if everything goes according to plan, there's no reason for the Dodgers not to use Scott in the ninth inning.
This is a guy who was tied for 14th in the league with his 25 saves, and he has a WHIP under 1.00 (0.99) which is incredibly impressive.
Regardless, Scott has picked up a save in his last three appearances. He's coming into the NLDS well-rested, and that's even with him earning a pair of saves at the end of the Dodgers regular season.
Keep in mind, Scott's last four appearances were all against the sub-par San Francisco Giants, and he did blow a pair of saves in the month of September.

Whenever the Los Angeles Dodgers playoff journey ends, they'll need to make several decisions on how to fortifiy the bullpen. Much like playoff time last season, the unit has become a house of cards that feels as if it's on the verge of collapse, even if there's been good news recently.
One player who won't be part of the postseason bullpen is veteran right-hander Blake Treinen. He suffered a shoulder injury while warming up in the bullpen during September 26's matchup against the San Francisco Giants. The full extent isn't yet known, but it is significant enough for the Dodgers to announce that the 38-year-old is done for the year.
Treinen is a free-agent-to-be, and that sets the scene for Los Angeles to make a decision. Does the club let the long-time high-leverage hurler walk? Or does the team follow the route it took with Evan Phillips, whom they re-signed while he was recovering from Tommy John surgery, with hopes that he could return as an impact bullpen arm down the stretch?
It's time for the Dodgers to thank Blake Treinen for his service and let him ride off into the sunset
Listening to some of his peers talk about the injury, it's clear that Treinen is a well-liked and influential player within the Dodgers' bullpen.
“It’s gut-wrenching for us,” Alex Vesia said, via Jack Harris of the California Post. “Blake’s one of our leaders out there in the bullpen.”
We're not going to say that veteran leadership doesn't matter, but there are a few key differences between Treinen's situation and the circumstances surrounding Phillips at the time that LA decided to bring him back.
The first has to do with age. Phillips is six years younger, and that matters. If Treinen were to come back and try to pitch in 2027, it would be for his age-39 season, making it extremely questionable as to whether or not he'd have anything left in the tank.
Timing matters too. As we saw with Phillips this year, it can take a bit for an injured reliever to get back into the groove. The 32-year-old was horrendous when he came back in July, throwing 7⅓ innings and surrendering five earned runs, including four home runs, before settling in to post a 2.41 over his final 18⅔ innings from August 1 onward. Even then, he didn't fully hit his stride until September.
The injuries these two relievers have suffered are different, but the thought remains the same. Treinen was also up and down this year, posting a decent 3.64 ERA, which means he might not have that extra gear that Phillips does.
The most important difference, however, is that Phillips had been mostly healthy before his UCL injury, whereas Treinen has dealt with a variety of maladies in recent years. He was limited to just 29⅔ innings this season and missed nearly two months with elbow inflammation. He dealt with forearm soreness in 2025 that limited him to just 26⅔ innings, dealt with a hip issue in 2024, and missed the entire 2023 campaign after undergoing shoulder surgery to repair his labrum and rotator cuff.
In fact, Treinen hasn't had a fully healthy year since 2021, so while he's put together dominant campaigns in the past, it's hard to expect him to be that same pitcher and avoid other injuries moving forward.
This should also be a lesson for the Dodgers, who have spent big on veteran relievers only to get mediocre results and a bunch of injuries. Relievers are volatile, and we saw that from Tanner Scott last year. We saw how quickly they can run out of gas with the Kirby Yates experiment. We're in the throes of it right now with Edwin Diaz.
The lesson from Phillips should be clear. Los Angeles originally acquired him off waivers from the Tampa Bay Rays in 2021. The Dodgers got him as a young player and made him into what he is today through their coaching and development plan. They need more of that and less star chasing in the pen, because the latter is more often than not a disappointment.

Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

Last week, Alex Vesia made sure to take in the scene.
A full month of baseball, he and the Dodgers hope, still lies ahead this October. Their game last Thursday was nothing more than a regular-season home finale, with the club set to open its postseason back at Dodger Stadium on Saturday in the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
Still, Vesia couldn’t help but feel sentimental as he traversed the clubhouse that afternoon, and sat out in the bullpen with several longtime teammates that night.
For the last six years, this has been home for the left-handed reliever.
As a pending free agent this offseason, it might not be much longer.
“I sent a text in our family group chat that was like, ‘I potentially could have played my last home game as a Dodger, in the regular season,’” Vesia recounted to the California Post this week. “And it was just like, damn.”
Vesia might not be one of the biggest stars of the Dodgers’ modern-day dynasty. But few players have been more important, or reliable, in their ascent to superteam status.
Since arriving as a little-known trade acquisition in February 2021 (acquired from the Miami Marlins, along with Kyle Hurt, in exchange for Dylan Floro), Vesia has been a stalwart in the Dodgers’ bullpen.
He has made 367 appearances for the club, a whopping 150 more than any other Dodgers pitcher in that span (Evan Phillips is next closest at 232). He has posted a 2.66 ERA and 5.7 wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs (ranking fifth among all left-handed relievers in the majors in that latter category during that period).
It was a rise that required personal reinvention, with the former 17th-round draft pick raising his arm slot and cultivating one of baseball’s most deceptive fastballs with the help of the organization’s highly-touted pitching department.
It was a road full of glorious highs, including two World Series championships, and gut-wrenching lows –– both on the field, like when he was optioned to the minor leagues for part of 2023, but especially off of it, after the unimaginable loss he and his wife experienced last October when their newborn daughter passed away during the Fall Classic.
That ordeal has changed the 30-year-old, in ways he still can’t fully verbalize yet.
“It’s been an extremely hard year,” Vesia said, with a set of pink-accented gloves honoring his late daughter resting in his locker behind him.
It has also altered his perspective during what might be his final ride in Los Angeles, making every little moment something to cherish ahead of an uncertain future.
“I’ve learned, especially over the last year, there’s certain moments in life that you need to stop and take it in,” he explained.
Vesia, of course, would love to be back with the Dodgers next year, and beyond. His consistent production and energetic mound presence have made him something of a fan favorite at this point; so much so, a local artist recently unveiled a mural of him in Burbank.
“I’m very thankful to have spent the last six years here,” he said. “I’ve learned so much about myself and the game, just what it takes to be a champion. That’s really, really, really special.”
Still, this lockout-threatened winter raises even more unknowns than usual.
Thus, even though he noted that “there’s still so much in front of us” this postseason, Vesia has allowed some nostalgia to creep in too.
“Even with Miggy and his sort of goodbye to baseball,” Vesia said, referencing likely-to-retire teammate Miguel Rojas, “some of the stuff that he has said about this team, I also resonate with. Like, it hits me too.”
Entering this October, Vesia’s bonds in the clubhouse and, especially, the bullpen –– a group he was first to nickname “The Dawgs” during their heroic contributions to the team’s 2024 title –– have never felt stronger.
Since the beginning of the season, he has been effusive in describing the ways they have supported him in the wake of last year’s tragedy.
In recent weeks, he has felt the unit’s performance collectively click into place, too, with the Dodgers’ relief corps emerging as a potentially underrated strength in their bid for a World Series three-peat.
“It was just like, guys got out of certain innings where … you could just see them start to trust their stuff,” Vesia said. “It’s definitely exciting. I think our guys in the bullpen are catching strides at the right time.”
Per usual, Vesia has been a key part of that resurgence. He posted a 2.64 ERA with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings on the season. More importantly, he improved his previously faulty command down the stretch, walking just one batter in 11 appearances during September.
Now, he’s hoping it sets up a storybook ending to what has been an emotional campaign –– and potentially his impactful Dodgers career.
“The way I view things are a little bit different. The way I go about my business is a little bit different. The way I’m motivated is a little bit different,” he said, while reflecting back on a traumatic 12 months that have made his connections in the organization all the more meaningful.
“Ultimately, I know the job that I have to do,” he added. “But yeah, my motivation for this month is different.”

The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

Over the last two months of the regular season, no team had a more productive bullpen than the Dodgers.
And come the start of their postseason trek on Saturday, the team might be adding another key arm back to the group.
General manager Brandon Gomes announced on Tuesday that the club expects to have hard-throwing right-handed reliever Edgardo Henriquez available for its National League Division Series, an encouraging development after Henriquez missed the final couple weeks of the regular season with a strain in his back.
Prior to getting hurt, Henriquez was emerging as one of the top arms in the Dodgers’ resurgent relief corps (which led all MLB bullpens in August and September with 4.3 combined wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs, and ranked fourth in that stretch in combined ERA at 3.20).
A 24-year-old former prospect who has started to routinely eclipse 103 mph with his fastball, Henriquez ranked fourth among the team’s relievers (minimum 20 appearances) with a 2.85 ERA this season. He also struck out 70 batters in 60 total innings and converted each of the ninth-inning save opportunities he received.
Henriquez had hit his stride in August and early September, allowing just one run in a 17-game stretch that featured 25 strikeouts and only two walks and seven hits allowed.
However, after giving up two runs in a Sept. 13 appearance in Miami against the Marlins, he went on the IL with his back injury –– one that initially cast doubt on his postseason availability.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez’s status has improved since then. He resumed a throwing during the team’s final regular-season homestand. He recently completed a session of live batting practice without feeling any lingering discomfort. And while Gomes said “we still got a few steps to go” before Henriquez gets the green light to return, every indication is that he should be available for the club’s best-of-five NLDS.
“If that all goes well, then yeah, the expectation is he’ll be on the roster,” Gomes said.
“Given the body of work, what he’s done, the unique skill set, that could be huge for us,” manager Dave Roberts added, before correcting himself: “Will be huge for us.”
Indeed, Henriquez would figure to occupy a high-leverage spot in the Dodgers’ postseason bullpen. He gives them not only a trustworthy right-hander option –– along with Roki Sasaki, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart and the recently resurgent Edwin Díaz –– but also one of the biggest fastballs in the game.
Henriquez’s 100.7 mph average fastball velocity ranked second among MLB pitchers this season, behind only star Padres closer Mason Miller. The team’s next-hardest thrower is Sasaki, whose heater averaged only 97.9 mph this year (though could increase in the playoffs as he shifts to a bullpen role).
Last October, Henriquez was a mixed bag in the playoffs. In two of his appearances (Game 1 of the wild card series and Game 5 of the World Series), he failed to record an out while allowing a hit and two walks in both outings. But in the other (Game 3 of the World Series), he pitched two scoreless frames in the team’s marathon 18-inning win, becoming an unsung hero in their Fall Classic triumph.
This time, Henriquez is set for a prominent role, assuming he gets through one more session of live batting practice OK.
“[He would make a] huge impact,” Roberts said. “I think he’s one of those guys that getting the bye has really benefited.”

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
-
- The Dodgers enter October seeking a third straight World Series title, but the club has not settled on a closer despite spending heavily on Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott.
- Andrew Friedman is confident about the Dodgers’ bullpen adapting to late-inning, high-leverage situations in the playoffs no matter who might be called upon.
SAN FRANCISCO — Stop me if you’ve heard this a million times, but the Dodgers are trying to become the first team to win three consecutive World Series championships since the New York Yankees, from 1998 to 2000.
Those Yankees had a Hall of Fame closer. In 1998, Mariano Rivera got the final four outs of the clincher. In 1999, he got the final four outs. In 2000, he got the final three outs.
These Dodgers? Their closer? Your guess is as good as theirs.
“I do not know,” said Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers’ president of baseball operations.
This might be a good time to know, no? The regular season is over. The postseason is upon us.
Alex Call hits a run-scoring double and Andy Pages follows with a three-run home run in the 10th inning of the Dodgers’ 5-1 win over the San Francisco Giants.
“I feel very confident that we’re going to be going into October with arguably the deepest and best pitching staff that we’ve had,” he said. “Exactly what their roles will be and how things will be ordered, I don’t know right now.”
Perhaps the Dodgers are overthinking this. They have done that before.
Tanner Scott converted 25 of 29 save opportunities this season, including saves Friday and Saturday.
But the strongest hitters on the Dodgers’ possible division series opponents are left-handed — Matt Olson, Drake Baldwin and Michael Harris II on the Atlanta Braves; Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber on the Philadelphia Phillies — and the Dodgers may not hesitate to use the left-handed Scott against those guys in the seventh or eighth inning.
In theory, these Dodgers have three candidates as closer: Scott, their marquee closer signing for 2025 and actual closer for most of 2026; Edwin Díaz, their marquee closer signing for 2026; and Roki Sasaki, their accidental closer last October.
Yet Friedman said he could envision scenarios where Evan Phillips could close, or even Brock Stewart, or perhaps Alex Vesia against a run of left-handed hitters. The Dodgers hope to activate Edgardo Henriquez for the playoffs. The starters could close, too, especially a well-rested Tyler Glasnow early in the first round.
Dave Roberts know the Dodgers’ chances of a three-peat rest on a surprise hero giving the team a timely boost. Meet Bill Plaschke’s top candidates for the job.
“We’ve got a number of guys that we really trust,” Friedman said. “Depending on who we’re playing, how deep our starter goes, there are a lot of factors that would go into it. But, more than who will be that pitcher on the mound, is the fact that we have so many candidates we feel really good about.”
That the Dodgers have improvised an October relief corps, transformed a rookie starter into a postseason closer and run bullpen games in elimination games might lead you to conclude Friedman does not really believe in the concept of a designated closer. In a world where “high leverage” is the trendy jargon, maybe a closer is more of an anachronism than a necessity.
That the Dodgers invested $72 million in Scott and $69 million in Díaz in consecutive winters would lead you to conclude Friedman does indeed believe in the concept of a designated closer. In fact, he does.
“I think it’s extremely helpful,” he said.
The Dodgers do not hold splashy news conferences to introduce closer candidates. When the Dodgers introduced Díaz last December, Friedman proudly introduced the three-time All-Star as the closer.
“For us, we have a high bar,” Friedman said then. “To name someone the closer, you have to be one of the best. You have to be elite and dominant at what you do.”
Díaz’s season went awry, limited to 18⅔ innings after elbow surgery and then a neck injury. But in five September appearances since his activation from the injured list, he gave up no runs and one hit in five innings, striking out nine of the 17 batters he faced. (In the same span, Scott has given up no runs and two hits in five innings, striking out nine of the 19 batters he faced.)
“What we’ve seen out of Díaz recently has been really encouraging,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “What that ultimately means, we don’t know yet.
“Of course, if you have a reliever who is really hot in October, that can be extremely valuable. It doesn’t mean you use him exclusively in the ninth. But, by and large, that’s how you would use him.”
Roberts saluted Díaz for working hard to get back to an uncertain assignment.
“I’m really proud of Edwin, given the deal he signed, to work it out, to go to the minors, to come back and pitch in whatever role we ask of him, that shows a lot of character,” Roberts said.
“He could have mailed this year in. That’s something that has not gone unnoticed. And we’ll see how October plays out.”
The Dodgers could be forgiven for believing it will all work out in the end. Their final pitcher in each of the World Series clinchers under Friedman, all starters: Julio Urías in 2020, Walker Buehler in 2024, Yoshinobu Yamamoto in 2025.
The pitchers to record a postseason save in those championship seasons: Kenley Jansen, Joe Kelly, Brusdar Graterol, Blake Treinen and Urias in 2020; Alex Vesia, Treinen and Buehler in 2024; Glasnow, Sasaki and Treinen in 2025.
The organizational flexibility can lead to some uncomfortable discussions within the clubhouse, as Roberts and coaches keep the relievers updated on the latest plan for how they might be used.
“It is tricky,” Roberts said. “These are constant conversations. They are ever-evolving. They are ongoing.”
If all goes right for the Dodgers, those conversations will be ongoing for another month.

SAN FRANCISCO — It was a four-inning wellness check.
Pitching for the first time since he left his start in Cincinnati after one inning with groin muscle discomfort, Blake Snell passed his test. He allowed one run on five hits in his four innings Saturday afternoon as the Dodgers beat the San Francisco Giants 4-3 on Kiké Hernandez’s ninth-inning home run.
The Dodgers will finish the season with a chance to reach 100 victories for the first time since 2023 – but the fourth time in the past six seasons and sixth time in the past nine full seasons.
Snell was healthy if not efficient. He threw 77 pitches to get through his four innings, allowing hits in each inning.
“Definitely needed to pitch today. Definitely showed that,” Snell said. “I was trying to go up and in, I was missing up and away. Even the last pitch of the game, I try to go up and in and miss right down the middle. I don’t know the last time I did that. It’s been a while. Even the changeup, the speed was up to 88. I gotta fix that as well. Get that to 86. Curveball, the release just has to get better.
“But overall, I learned a lot from it. Really encouraged by it, and just happy to get my legs underneath me and get going and completely move past the groin. I mean, it felt great today, and the velo was good. … I’ve got to figure my body out a little more, but I got a week to do so, and I’m really looking forward to that.”
He stranded runners at the corners in the first inning and at second base in the second. Jonah Cox led off the third with a double into the left-field corner, stole third and scored on a sacrifice fly. Snell gave up a two-out single in the fourth, but Shay Whitcomb was thrown out by left fielder Teoscar Hernandez when he tried to stretch it into a double.
After the game in Cincinnati, Snell expressed confidence that he had avoided serious injury by recognizing the signs early and coming out of the game – something he didn’t do before landing on the injured list four previous times with groin injuries.
Saturday supported that decision. Snell’s fastball averaged 96.8 mph (up slightly from his season average) and he got 10 swings-and-misses (though only three strikeouts). Snell now lines up as the likely Game 3 starter in the National League Division Series, giving him over a week before his next start.
“I thought the fastball was had life. Just some near misses to kind of flip counts,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “The changeup was okay. The curveball I thought was good. But I think for him overall, he just wasn’t as efficient as he wanted, as we wanted. But again, I thought it was fine for his last tune-up for the postseason.
“I was confident, we were confident (that Snell was healthy). But I think it’s still good to see it. And it’s good also that we got it out of the way, got that rust off, versus whatever game in the postseason, then he’s rusty, and you’ve got to kind of pick up the pieces in a playoff game. So I thought today it was again, really best-case scenario.”
The Dodgers’ offense gave Snell a 3-1 lead.
Mookie Betts hit a solo home run in the third inning – his seventh home run in September as he surges over the final month of the season. Four singles and a walk produced two more runs in the fourth inning.
After a two-hit game including an RBI double Thursday, Shohei Ohtani has gone 1 for 9 with five strikeouts in the two games against the Giants. The lone hit was a ground ball under the glove of Giants first baseman Brett Harris in the fourth inning that was originally ruled an error and later changed.
“I thought today there was just more chase,” Roberts said of Ohtani’s 1 for 5. “And I don’t know if he’s trying to get hits, find his swing, getting a little over-anxious. Everything from Shohei to the training staff, the hitting guys, the work has been great. Looks exactly like it did, like it’s supposed to look.”
Roberts dismissed any suggestion that Ohtani is still not healthy after spending two weeks on the injured list.
“I don’t see any wincing. The bat speed is still (good),” Roberts said. “There’s one thing to just say you could just put him on ice and hope that the performance is there Game One of the postseason, or there’s another camp that says everything looks right and you have to get him (at-bats) and it’s still only – what is it 12, 13 at bats, 14 at bats (since he returned)? So, with a long layoff, that’s not easy either to come back and perform.”
The Dodgers’ bullpen couldn’t hold the 3-1 lead. The Giants came back to tie it with single runs against Brock Stewart in the seventh and Evan Phillips in the eighth before Hernandez put the Dodgers back in the lead with a leadoff home run in the ninth.
The homer was an uplifting moment in a difficult season for Hernandez, who started the season on the IL following elbow surgery, returned for two games, then missed two months with an oblique injury.
“Yeah, I mean it’s been tough, but I mean, it is what it is,” Hernandez said. “That’s the card I’ve drawn this year. It’s nobody’s fault. I was expected to miss the first couple months because of my rehab, and then I was not expecting to miss more time so quickly after coming back. It just happened to be that way. And when you have a team like this one, it’s hard getting in the lineup. So it’s just one of those things where that’s what you have, and you got to make the best of it. I just happened to not have made the best of my opportunities this year.”

Bo Davidson hit a tying sacrifice fly off Evan Phillips (3-2) with two outs in the eighth for San Francisco before Hernández answered against Trent Harris (0-1) for his fourth homer.

Betts homered with two outs in the third inning for his team's first hit before Miguel Rojas and Tommy Edman added RBI singles the next two innings.
Betts' blast to the bleachers in left-center sent the large contingent of Dodgers fans in the sellout crowd of 40,124 at Oracle Park into a frenzy on a beautiful sunny afternoon in the Bay Area.
Shohei Ohtani, playing for a fourth straight day following a 13-game absence with right biceps discomfort, went 1 for 5 with two strikeouts after an 0-for-4 showing with three Ks on Friday night.
When Camilo Doval pitched the seventh for San Francisco, he became the 71st player used by the club this season - matching Atlanta's MLB record set last year.
Los Angeles left-hander Blake Snell struck out three and didn't walk a batter, allowing one run on five hits over four innings in his final playoff tune-up.
The Giants lost their fourth straight, seventh of eight and seventh in a row to the rival Dodgers after taking four of five in the series to start the year.
Los Angeles earned its 14th shutout of the season in a 2-0 win Friday, then manager Dave Roberts rested first baseman Freddie Freeman and gave Hernández a start. The Dodgers improved their majors-best road record to 48-32.
Up next
Neither team had announced its starter for Sunday's regular-season finale, when beloved Giants broadcaster Mike Krukow will be celebrated before he retires from the booth after nearly four decades.

Blake Snell looked healthy in his final regular season start and Kiké Hernández homered in the ninth inning to give the Dodgers a 4-3 win over the Giants on Saturday afternoon at Oracle Park in San Francisco.
Snell allowed only one run in his four innings and at the very least showed no limitations from leaving his start with left groin tightness on September 16 in Cincinnati. The Dodgers weren’t going to push Snell on Saturday, but more wanted to make sure he got one more start in before the postseason starts in a week.
“If he can go five innings and come out of it feeling great, that would be fantastic,” manager Dave Roberts told reporters at Oracle Park earlier Saturday, as shown on SportsNet LA. “There’s a balance between getting your work in and making sure you feel good coming out of it.”
Snell threw 77 pitches in his four innings so he wasn’t all that efficient, though he didn’t walk anyone and threw his two fastest pitches of the season — first-inning fastballs at 98.6 mph and 98.2 mph — while averaging 96.8 mph on the fastball on Saturday.
The lone run came when Jonah Cox doubled to open the third inning, stole third base, and scored on a sacrifice fly.
San Francisco swiped two bases Saturday off Snell, who has allowed 10 steals in his nine starts this season. But Snell has limited the damage by simply not allowing many people to reach, with only 25 hits and 14 walks in 39 2/3 innings, a .260 on-base percentage since returning from the injured list.
Snell since returning allowed only five runs, never more than one in any start. On the season he did not allow a home run, his 42 2/3 innings the seventh-most by a Dodgers pitcher in the live-ball era without giving up a long ball.

The rookie left-hander, who pitched five scoreless innings in Los Angeles before the Dodgers scored single runs in the next three innings to complete a weekend sweep, on Saturday held the Dodgers without a run until Mookie Betts hit one into the left field seats in the third inning.
Betts has seven home runs in September, after hitting five combined home runs in July and August. It’s been a month to remember for Betts, who raised his seasonal OPS from .701 at the start of September to .783 now, with just one day remaining in the regular season.
Wilkinson was done after three innings, and the Dodgers immediately responded with four singles and a walk in the fourth inning to score two runs.
San Francisco clawed back with single runs in the seventh and eighth innings, before Hernández took Trent Harris deep to open the ninth inning.
Treinen hurt?
Brock Stewart pitched the bottom of the seventh inning but was allotted extra warm-up pitches as he entered the game. He wasn’t warming up in the bullpen before getting called in, but Blake Treinen was before suddenly stopping. In the top of the eighth, the SportsNet LA broadcast showed footage from the Dodgers bullpen, showing bullpen coach Josh Bard embracing Treinen, then of Treinen walking back to the Dodgers dugout and clubhouse with trainer Bernard Li.
Treinen missed two and a half months with elbow inflammation before returning in September, when he has allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings, with three walks and six strikeouts.

Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez provided an update on his back injury, which has him on the injured list and makes his postseason status uncertain.
Edgardo Henriquez’s injury progress
Henriquez told The Athletic’s Fabian Aradaya that he threw a bullpen session on Wednesday, September 24th, his first since being placed on the injured list.
He feels like his back is in a better spot, and that he can get ready for the National League Division Series on Saturday, October 3rd.
The Dodgers put Henriquez on the 15-day injured list a little more than a week ago with a low-grade back strain, manager Dave Roberts revealed.
When he placed Henriquez on the injured list, Roberts was “hopeful” Henriquez would be back for the postseason.
The MRI, according to him, was “positive,” all things considered.
Thus far, things have played out accordingly, though the next week of recovery and rest will be the big test.
Why the Dodgers need Henriquez
Henriquez is the Dodgers’ most impressive right-handed reliever out of the bullpen.
He has a 2.62 ERA and a 2.50 FIP, and his profile is ideal for postseason baseball. He misses the barrel of the bat, strikes out hitters, and limits home runs, with command being the determining factor in his outing go.
Luckily for the Dodgers, Henriquez has figured out his control well enough that it hasn’t been a problem this year.
Compared to Edwin Diaz, Henriquez is much more reliable, while Brock Stewart and Evan Phillips are better suited for middle-relief chances.
If healthy, Henriquez should get save chances, with Roki Sasaki and Tanner Scott right in the mix as well. Diaz has started to creep up in the mix, but Henriquez has the confidence and demeanor to take command of the role.

Tuesday night’s game against the San Diego Padres was reminiscent of the 2024 playoffs when the Dodgers were forced to employ a bullpen in the NLDS to keep their playoff hopes alive against those same Padres. Both outcomes were the same, with the bullpen shutting down the Friars and getting a big win.
That postseason saw a lot of bullpen usage, and in this one the Dodgers are stacked with starters. Still, the bullpen is always a big part of the postseason.
As Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic points out, 41 days ago manager Dave Roberts was asking the media what choices did he truly have to deploy in the ninth inning of games. Now, he could have several options.
Edwin Diaz, the closer they paid handsomely in the offseason, has not had a great season. He’s been on the IL twice and had an era over 11.00 at one point this summer. But since returning from his latest IL stint, he has faced 11 batters, struck out six and only allowed two to reach base.
“I think it’s one of those things where if you’re one of the 12 pitchers on a postseason roster, you’re in the trust tree,” Roberts said “He’s put himself right smack in that conversation. Given all that he’s had to go through this year to right the ship is a big credit to him.”
Roki Sasaki is also someone who will be in the mix for the ninth inning spot. He has also just returned from his own IL stint, pitching with dermabond on his blister. He allowed two singles, but worked around them for a scoreless inning in Tuesday night’s game. He will appear in Friday night’s game as he continues to work towards a spot in the bullpen that will likely vary as the postseason goes on.
Tanner Scott has been the Dodgers’ most reliable arm out of the bullpen this season, and Roberts has remarked how it would be nice to be able to use Scott in high leverage spots that may not come just in the ninth inning.
“I think if there’s an opportunity, for example, for Tanner to pitch a high-leverage inning in the seventh or the eighth inning, it’s just hard to pass that up if he’s the best option right there,” Roberts said. “You just don’t know where the ninth inning is going to be.”
Roberts also added that the team is sitting in their best position with regards to the bullpen as they have ever been. Evan Phillips and Brock Stewart round out the current options, and the team hopes that Edguardo Henriquez can recover from his back issues to appear in the playoffs. With the starters this team has overall this may be the best pitching staff the Dodgers have ever sent to the playoffs.

LOS ANGELES — A quad injury cost Jason Adam the chance to help the Padres in last year’s NL Wild Card Series. The team is intent on seeing what the 35-year-old veteran can provide this time around.
Out since late June with a shoulder injury, Adam was activated ahead of Wednesday’s 7:10 p.m. start at Dodger Stadium. To make room, right-hander Griffin Canning was optioned to Triple-A El Paso and reliever Alek Jacob was designated for assignment to allow Adam to rejoin the 40-man roster.
“We saw last year when he got hurt how much we missed him just within the team dynamic and what he provides as experience out there in the bullpen,” Padres manager Craig Stammen said. “We’ve got a lot more experience than what we had last year in the bullpen right now with those guys being together. But Jason’s a big part of that. He’s a big part of that group out there, and then he’s a pretty darn good pitcher also.”
A first-time All-Star last year, Adam allowed nine runs on seven hits and two walks over 1⅓ innings across three rehab appearances with El Paso. But both he and the team were satisfied with the stuff he showed in hitter-friendly conditions, as well as in live batting practice on Monday, and added his experience to a bullpen that was a strength last year and this year.
Adam’s velocity has trended down from about 95 mph the year the Padres acquired him in 2024 (1.95 ERA) to 94 mph last year (1.93 ERA) to 93 mph this year (2.51 ERA). He missed time earlier in the year as he returned from last year’s season-ending quad surgery and said Tuesday he was eager to get back in the thick of a postseason push.
“Yeah, I’d love to be part of every game,” Adam said after joining the team at Dodger Stadium on Tuesday. “What this team’s doing is really special. So I just want to fill my role, however that looks, and help them win ballgames. We’ve seen pretty well that this team’s good with or without me. I just want to do my part to contribute.”
Ousted from the rotation earlier this summer, Canning was better as a reliever (3.82 ERA in 35⅓ innings) than as a starter (6.79 ERA in 50 ⅓ innings) and had been critical in helping the team piece together games ahead of the trade deadline. But the team only needs three starters for the NL Wild Card Series, he was behind the likes of Robbie Ray, Casey Mize and Randy Vásquez in terms of depth arms for a short series and David Morgan has allowed one run in his last 7⅔ innings to seemingly cement his spot in the depth chart ahead of Canning.
The Padres optioning Canning to the minors means he cannot return to the active roster without an injury until the middle of the NL Division Series, after 15 days.
Jacob, 28, had a 5.58 ERA in 61⅓ innings at Triple-A El Paso and 4.18 ERA in 56 innings across parts of four seasons in the majors. He pitched in three games this year, allowing three runs in five innings as an up-and-down arm.
Ohtani returns, Salas starts
As expected the Dodgers reinstated Shohei Ohtani (biceps, knee from the injured list, as well as left-hander Tarik Skubal from the bereavement list. To make room, outfielder Josue De Paula and Hurt were optioned to Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Ohtani will bat second and serve as the designated hitter for the Dodgers, who have won eight of 11 so far against the Padres this year. Ohtani was 0-for-3 when he last played on Sept. 9 and was in a .122/.295/.184 slide over his last 13 games.

As for the Padres, Ethan Salas will get his first start at Dodger Stadium and second pairing with left-hander Robbie Ray. The only starter he has not worked with is Michael King.
Salas (.627 OPS) was 1-for-2 off the bench on Tuesday. He will bat ninth in a lineup that will see Samad Taylor (.856 OPS) get the start as the DH after Austin Hays did so on Tuesday.

While the Padres’ lead on the Diamondbacks was shaved from five to four games with five games left in the season — including three head-to-head matches in San Diego — Tuesday’s loss did little to diminish postseason odds, which are at 93.5% according to FanGraphs.com.
As was the case on Tuesday, any combination of two Padres wins and/or Diamondbacks losses will clinch the team’s third straight postseason berth.
Right-hander Merrill Kelly (9-14, 5.00 ERA) will start at Coors Field for Arizona against Rockies right-hander Mason Adams (0-1, 5.09 ERA). First pitch there is 5:40 p.m..
The Padres, Cubs and Phillies all began Wednesday with identical 87-70 records, although the Padres have to finish ahead of both teams to earn home games in the NL Wild Card Series as they lost both season series.
The Dodgers’ magic number to clinch a first-round bye over the Braves is 1. They are also one game ahead of the Brewers in the race for the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Glass half full
The Dodgers just about emptied the bullpen in Tuesday’s 7-0 win over the Padres. In the aftermath of another bullpen game slowing an offense that ranks first in the majors this month in OPS (.835), a half-glass-full view of what transpired was worth taking forward.
The Padres saw all but two relievers — Kris Bubic and Evan Phillips — in their first shutout loss since Aug. 25 and they still had two more games to wade through in Chavez Ravine.
“They’re really good bullpen arms, so the more you can see them, the better shot you have,” first baseman Ty France said late Tuesday night. “But just move on to (Wednesday) and try to put some better at-bats together.”
The challenge of a bullpen game is a hitter rarely sees a pitcher twice and the Padres are especially proficient when they see relievers more than once.
They rank 10th in the majors with a .712 OPS against relievers, but 17th the first time they see a reliever (.704) and first the second time they see a reliever (.998 OPS).
Right-hander Kyle Hurt was the only pitcher to finish two innings and he allowed just one hit and faced seven batters while taking down the sixth and seventh innings.
Left-hander Jack Dreyer and right-hander Edwin Diaz got through their frames without giving up a baserunner. The rest of the slate of relievers all faced five batters or less.
In short, things went about as optimal as the Dodgers could hope for from a unit ranks 12th in the majors with a 3.82 ERA.
“The Dodgers bullpen’s got some good arms in it,” Stammen said. “They’re bringing out guys that have really good stuff. But the best way to do it is to play a little small ball and try to beat them that way. We just didn’t have the opportunity to play that way and score one run at a time (after) we get down 4-0. That kind of eliminates that way of playing baseball. But you know, we’ve seen their arms now for the rest of the series, and hopefully that benefits us going forward the next two days.”

He’s got a 5.22 ERA in eight starts since the trade deadline. His last start (6 IP, 3 ER) was one of three quality starts as a Padre and a 6-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio was his best since the trade. Ray has a 3.81 ERA in 26 career starts against the Dodgers, but he has allowed 15 earned runs in 19 ⅓ runs over four starts over the last two years.
